questions.prompt: Where does a text-to-image diffusion model start when generating a new image?
questions.explanation: Generation starts from random Gaussian noise (in pixel or latent space) and denoises step by step. It does not retrieve or copy a stored image.

questions.prompt: In the forward diffusion process, the amount of original signal in x_t decreases as t increases.
questions.explanation: The signal weight sqrt(alpha_bar_t) shrinks towards zero as noise accumulates, so late steps are almost pure noise.

options: An open standard for signed content provenance manifests (Content Credentials)
questions.explanation: C2PA is a standard from the Coalition for Content Provenance and Authenticity for cryptographically signed metadata about how content was made and edited. It is not a sampler, metric or model.

questions.prompt: What does this classifier-free guidance code print?
questions.code:
eps_uncond, eps_cond, w = 0.1, 0.3, 5.5
print(round(eps_uncond + w * (eps_cond - eps_uncond), 2))
questions.explanation: guided = 0.1 + 5.5 * (0.3 - 0.1) = 0.1 + 1.1 = 1.2 (shown rounded). 0.3 is the plain conditional prediction (w = 1), and the others are arithmetic slips.

questions.prompt: Mode collapse, where the model produces only a narrow range of outputs, is most associated with which family?
questions.explanation: GAN generators can learn to fool the discriminator with a few output types, losing diversity. Diffusion models are known for stable training and good diversity, which is one reason they replaced GANs for many tasks.

questions.prompt: Which are known limits of CLIP score as an evaluation metric? Select all that apply.
options: Weak at spatial relations such as left of / right of
Inherits biases of the CLIP model
Requires the real training images to compute
questions.explanation: CLIP score compares image and prompt embeddings, so it inherits CLIP's blind spots and biases. It needs only the generated image and its prompt, unlike FID, which needs a reference set of real images.

questions.prompt: Two engineers compare model A and model B with 10 prompts each but different seeds, step counts and guidance scales. B looks better. What is wrong with the comparison?
options: Too many variables changed at once; fix seeds, sampler, steps, guidance and size so the model is the only difference, and use more prompts and raters
They should have used FID on 10 images
They should only compare file sizes
questions.explanation: A fair comparison controls everything except the model. FID on 10 images is statistically meaningless, and file size says nothing about quality.

questions.prompt: Generated images have valid C2PA manifests at the API, but downloads from your web app show 'no content credentials'. The pipeline is: generate -> sign -> resize -> compress -> store. What is the most likely fix?
options: Sign after the final resize and compression step, or use processing tools that preserve and update the manifest
questions.explanation: Re-encoding after signing drops or invalidates the manifest. Signing last (or using C2PA-aware tools that record the edits) fixes it. Safety filters, guidance and file format choice do not address lost metadata.

questions.prompt: A bias audit generates 'a photo of a nurse' 100 times and 95 images show women. The product team says each image is fine individually. What is the best response?
options: Agree; individual images are fine so there is no issue
Treat it as a distribution-level harm: document it, test mitigations such as prompt diversification, and track the distribution as a release metric
questions.explanation: Representational bias appears only across many samples, which is exactly why audits run many seeds. Mitigate and measure. Banning words or lowering resolution avoids or ignores the problem.

questions.prompt: Why does latent diffusion's autoencoder matter for testing fine details such as small text in images?
options: It does not affect output at all
Detail must survive compression into the latent and decoding back, so the autoencoder can limit fine detail regardless of how good the denoiser is
questions.explanation: The decoder reconstructs pixels from a compressed latent, so very fine detail can be lost or garbled there. That is one reason small text rendering is a classic weak spot to test. It is not purely about speed and does not add watermarks.

coding.title: Compute alpha-bar for a noise schedule
coding.prompt:
Write `alpha_bars(betas)` that returns the cumulative products ᾱ_t = (1 − β₁)(1 − β₂)…(1 − β_t) as a list of the same length as `betas`.

Example: `alpha_bars([0.1, 0.5])` returns `[0.9, 0.45]`.
coding.explanation: Each step keeps a fraction (1 − β) of the signal, so the fraction left after t steps is the running product. This closed form lets training jump straight to any noise level.
hints: Keep a running product starting at 1.0.
Multiply by `(1 - b)` for each beta and append the product.

tests.name: Matches the example
tests.code:
r = alpha_bars([0.1, 0.5])
assert len(r) == 2 and abs(r[0] - 0.9) < 1e-9 and abs(r[1] - 0.45) < 1e-9, f'got {r}'

tests.name: Decreases monotonically towards zero
tests.code:
betas = [0.02] * 500
r = alpha_bars(betas)
assert len(r) == 500 and all(a > b for a, b in zip(r, r[1:])), 'should strictly decrease'
assert r[-1] < 0.0001, f'last value {r[-1]}'

coding.title: Noise and recover with a perfect noise prediction
coding.prompt:
Implement two functions for one value:

- `add_noise(x0, alpha_bar, eps)` returns `sqrt(alpha_bar) * x0 + sqrt(1 - alpha_bar) * eps`.
- `estimate_x0(xt, alpha_bar, eps_pred)` inverts it: returns `(xt - sqrt(1 - alpha_bar) * eps_pred) / sqrt(alpha_bar)`.

Raise `ValueError` in `estimate_x0` if `alpha_bar <= 0` (the signal is gone and x0 cannot be recovered).
coding.explanation: This is the DDPM closed form and its inverse. A trained network supplies eps_pred; the better its prediction, the better the estimate of the clean image, which is why training minimises the noise-prediction error.
hints: The inverse subtracts the noise term then divides by the signal weight.

tests.name: add_noise follows the closed form
tests.code:
r = add_noise(1.0, 0.64, 0.5)
assert r is not None and abs(r - (0.8 + 0.6 * 0.5)) < 1e-9, f'got {r}'

tests.name: Perfect prediction recovers x0
tests.code:
xt = add_noise(0.7, 0.3, -1.2)
r = estimate_x0(xt, 0.3, -1.2)
assert r is not None and abs(r - 0.7) < 1e-9, f'got {r}'

tests.name: Rejects alpha_bar of zero

coding.title: Prompt-suite regression report
coding.prompt:
You compare a candidate image model against a baseline using per-prompt scores (for example CLIP scores or mean human ratings). Write `regression_report(baseline, candidate, tolerance)` where both are dicts `{prompt: score}`.

Return a dict with:
- `regressed`: sorted list of prompts where `candidate < baseline - tolerance`
- `improved`: sorted list where `candidate > baseline + tolerance`
- `missing`: sorted list of baseline prompts absent from candidate
- `passed`: `True` only if nothing regressed and nothing is missing.
coding.explanation: Per-prompt comparison with a tolerance catches regressions that an average would hide, and treating missing prompts as failures stops a broken pipeline from silently passing. Regressed prompts then go to human review.
hints: Loop over the baseline so missing prompts are detected.

tests.name: Finds regressions and improvements
Missing prompts fail the run
tests.code:
r = regression_report({'a': 0.3, 'b': 0.3}, {'a': 0.3}, 0.01)
assert r.get('missing') == ['b'] and r.get('passed') is False, f'got {r}'

tests.name: Within tolerance passes
tests.code:
r = regression_report({'a': 0.30}, {'a': 0.29}, 0.02)
assert r == {'regressed': [], 'improved': [], 'missing': [], 'passed': True}, f'got {r}'
